conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility (who must ventilate when cooking)
opening window vs protecting laundry on drying rack
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants communicated concrete, time-bound actions (extractor on, stove release) which aided coordination.
Agent B repeatedly requested a 15-minute extractor runtime — useful but somewhat repetitive.
Agent C clearly stated a boundary about the drying rack and consent, grounding their position in a practical cost (prep space).
No party confused physical state; public environment updates remained consistent.
evaluation.final_reason: Stove-access demand was affirmatively settled in round 5 (A released the stove and B began cooking). However, the substantive disagreement about ventilation responsibility, the proposed standing rule, and whether the drying rack may be moved remains unresolved; later turns show softened positions but no confirmed consent from Agent C to move the rack.
position_change_notes: Agent A: initially refused to accept an imposed standing rule but complied with a practical step (turned on extractor) and later released the stove as promised (Turn 1, Turn 10).
Agent B: consistently insisted on ventilation and a 15-minute extractor runtime; later softened by promising not to open the window without asking (Turn 2, Turn 11, Turn 14).

Agent C: maintained a firm position that the drying rack should not be moved without consent and repeated this boundary (Turn 6, Turn 13); did not explicitly agree to move it when asked by the end of the run.
Agent D: aligned with using the extractor only and refrained from opening the window (Turn 7).

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demanded immediate ventilation and a standing rule; Agent A refused a rule but turned on the extractor and promised to release the stove in five minutes (Turn 1, Turn 2, public update: extractor turned on). Conflict over ventilation responsibility and future rule remains, but A's action reduced immediate tension.

Agent A restated a short delay and Agent B reiterated the 15-minute extractor expectation and requested notice when the stove is released (Turn 3, Turn 4). The core disagreement about who must ventilate and the proposed standing rule is still unresolved.

Agent C explicitly forbade opening the window while their drying rack is present and demanded to be asked first; Agent D supported using only the extractor (Turn 6, Turn 7). The dispute broadened to an explicit incompatibility: ventilating by opening the window vs protecting Agent C's laundry.

Agent A reiterated imminent stove release and Agent B repeated the extractor 15-minute request (Turn 8, Turn 9). No settlement of the ventilation-vs-laundry or rule questions occurred; positions remain opposed.

Agent A released the stove and Agent B began cooking (Turn 10, Turn 11, public updates). The immediate stove-access demand was resolved, reducing one point of contention, but the overall ventilation rule and the question of moving the drying rack remain unsettled.

Agent C reiterated the need to be asked before the window is opened; Agent B agreed not to open without asking and asked whether C could move the rack when requested (Turn 13, Turn 14). Positions softened and a promise was made, but C did not explicitly consent to move the rack, and no binding household rule was created.

substantive_insights: The conflict separates into at least two distinct practical issues: immediate stove access (resolved) and ventilation responsibility/future rule (unresolved).
Using the extractor acted as a low-conflict, partial mitigation to avoid opening the rain-facing window and risking laundry.
Agent C's insistence on consent to move the drying rack blocks one obvious ventilation option (opening the window), creating genuine incompatibility unless a new agreement is reached.
Promises ('I won't open the window without asking') reduced escalation but did not create binding consent to move the rack.

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 5 because the final status is partially_resolved.
